segments.text: Hello again.
Day nineteen.
By now you may go hours without a thought of it.
Whole afternoons.
And then, out of nowhere, one hits you.
Strong, sudden, as if no time had passed.
Someone lights up ahead of you on the street, and the smell reaches you.
And a worried thought follows it.
"I thought I was past this."
You are past the part you're thinking of.
This is something else.
Certain places, smells and moments can still set off a craving, even weeks after you stop.
Each time you get through one, that link tends to get weaker.
The first time in each new situation is often the hardest.
Think back to the autopilot.
For years, certain cues were paired with nicotine, over and over.
You've already worn down the everyday ones.
Your morning.
Your coffee.
Your drive.
But some cues only come round now and then.
A particular friend.
A certain bar.
The first warm evening of the year.
Those haven't had their turn yet.
So when one fires, it isn't the gap coming back.
It's an echo.
An old cue, meeting you for the first time since you stopped.
Let's rehearse meeting one.
Take a breath, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
Picture a place or a moment you haven't been in since you stopped.
Somewhere you always used.
Imagine the craving arriving.
Fast, and stronger than you expected.
Name it.
"Old cue."
Find it in your body, the way you know how.
And watch it like a wave.
It rises.
It peaks.
And it falls.
A craving rises, peaks and passes, usually within minutes.
This one is no different.
It only feels bigger because it surprised you.
You don't need a new tool for this.
You need the one you've used every day for nearly three weeks.
In a moment, you'll pick the cues that could catch you off guard, so they're less of a surprise when they come.
Old cue.
Same skill.
And smaller next time.
I'll see you in a couple of days.
